articles.title: How to Turn ChatGPT Images 2.5 into an API
articles.excerpt: I could already ask my agent to generate an image through MCP. But I wanted to try something less conversational: send a prompt from a script and get a file back. That was the gap I wanted a ChatGPT i…
articles.body: I could already ask my agent to generate an image through MCP. But I wanted to try something less conversational: send a prompt from a script and get a file back. That was the gap I wanted a ChatGPT image generation API to fill. No agent choosing a tool for me, and no manual download at the end. Just a request my code could submit and a result it could retrieve. The answer was in the BrowserAct ChatGPT image template I had already been using. Its published Bot could be called through HTTP as well as MCP. I tested that route with a perfume-bottle prompt and downloaded the resulting PNG. What interested me was having one reusable image tool: I could call it from code, use it from a compatible agent, and keep the ChatGPT login in one configured browser environment.

articles.body: On a Mac Studio M4 Max with 64 GB, Qwen3.8-27B with MTP does not replace the 35B mixture-of-experts model I already run. Measured on 12 October 2026 under oMLX 0.7.0, Qwen generated 55 tokens per second against 90, and took 3.46 seconds to produce its first token on an 800-token prompt against 0.49. On a code review test the two caught the same bugs with reasoning off, and Qwen caught fewer with it on. The number that decides it is time to first token Qwen3.8-27B needs seven times longer than Ornith 1.5 to start answering an 800-token prompt: 3.46 seconds against 0.49, averaged over 8 requests per model. Output speed is closer, 55.1 tokens per second against 90.4. In a chat that gap is a nuisance.

articles.title: Mastering Git Branches Like a Jedi: A Solo Dev's Quest
articles.excerpt: The Quest Begins (The “Why”) Honestly, I used to treat Git like a glorified undo button. I’d hack away at a feature for hours, then slap together one massive commit with a message like “fix stuff” or…
articles.body: The Quest Begins (The “Why”) Honestly, I used to treat Git like a glorified undo button. I’d hack away at a feature for hours, then slap together one massive commit with a message like “fix stuff” or “wip”. It felt productive—until I hit a bug that only showed up after midnight, and I had no idea which of the thirty‑plus changes I’d made was the culprit. I spent three hours bisecting manually, scrolling through diffs that looked like a scrambled Rubik’s Cube, and honestly felt like I was trying to find the One Ring in a pile of socks. That nightmare made me ask: What if I could make Git work for me instead of against me? I started digging into how the pros use version control, and the answer was surprisingly simple: atomic, descriptive commits .

articles.title: Icons injected by CSS stay silent for screen readers, so icon-only buttons still need a name
articles.excerpt: Every icon system eventually fails somebody. With icon fonts it was the screen reader user who heard a private-use codepoint read aloud, and the dyslexic reader whose font override wiped the icons out…
articles.body: Every icon system eventually fails somebody. With icon fonts it was the screen reader user who heard a private-use codepoint read aloud, and the dyslexic reader whose font override wiped the icons out. With inline SVG it is usually the reviewer, who has to dig the control's actual label out from under a wall of path data. Lea Verou's new post, "The best way to use icons in Web UIs", argues for a third route: keep icons entirely in CSS, and keep them out of the HTML. My question about any proposal like this is who it locks out. This one holds up better than I expected, provided you get one detail right. Who the old approaches let down Verou says the most common way to include icons today is inline SVG in the HTML.

articles.title: Your Nuxt layers are leaking, and your linter can't see it
articles.excerpt: Here is a Vue component. Spot the architecture bug. const cart = useCart(); Looks fine, right? No weird imports. Nothing red in the editor. ESLint is happy. The PR gets approved. The problem: useCart…
articles.body: Here is a Vue component. Spot the architecture bug. <!-- lyears/admin/app/components/AdminPanel.vue --> < script setup lang= "ts" > const cart = useCart (); </ script > < template > <CartSummary /> </ template > Looks fine, right? No weird imports. Nothing red in the editor. ESLint is happy. The PR gets approved. The problem: useCart and <CartSummary> live in the shop layer. The admin layer was never supposed to touch shop . You just tied two parts of your app together, and nobody noticed. Not you, not the reviewer, not a single tool in the pipeline. Do that thirty more times and your nice modular Nuxt app is one big ball of yarn with a layers/ folder on top.

articles.title: Incremental Indexing for Multi-Tenant Help Center Retrieval (and Freshness)
articles.excerpt: For a multi-tenant SaaS help center, the least complex design that stays explainable is a staged retrieval pipeline: explicit collections per isolation boundary, bounded queries, and source context ca…
articles.body: For a multi-tenant SaaS help center, the least complex design that stays explainable is a staged retrieval pipeline: explicit collections per isolation boundary, bounded queries, and source context carried all the way into the answer. Incremental indexing then becomes a freshness problem with a measurable contract, rather than a vague promise that “the vector store is up to date.” Short answer: define the retrieval unit and tenant filter first, index only changed units, and keep ingestion, querying, and citation as separate observable stages. Start with the retrieval contract Before choosing a database or endpoint, write down what a user-visible answer is allowed to use. A useful contract names the tenant, document revision, locale, product area, and an evidence span.

articles.title: The 'Halloween Fireballs' are coming. Here's what to expect from the Taurids this year
articles.excerpt: The Southern and Northern Taurid meteor showers will produce occasional bright, slow-moving meteors worldwide during October and November, with moon-free peaks in 2026.
articles.body: They don't produce anything like the torrent of "shooting stars" associated with August's Perseids or December's Geminids, but the Taurid meteor showers have something else going for them — fireballs. The Taurids are famous for occasionally producing exceptionally bright, slow-moving meteors that can streak dramatically across the night sky from September to December. As a bonus, they're visible from both the Northern and Southern hemispheres. That's because they appear to emanate from the constellation Taurus, which sits close to the ecliptic, the apparent path the sun takes across the sky as Earth orbits around it. The Taurids are actually two closely related showers — the Southern Taurids and Northern Taurids — whose activity overlaps in late October and November.

articles.title: On this day in space! Oct. 12, 1964: The Soviet Union launches Voskhod 1, the 1st multi-person cosmonaut crew, into space
articles.excerpt: On Oct. 12, 1964, the Soviet Union launched Voskhod 1, a 24-hour crewed mission that achieved several "firsts" for human spaceflight. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Oct. 12, 1964, the Soviet Union launched Voskhod 1, a 24-hour crewed mission that achieved several "firsts" for human spaceflight . This was the first time that a spacecraft carried more than one person into orbit, with three cosmonauts packed inside the spacecraft. Only two cosmonauts were originally supposed to fly on this mission, but Soviet politicians pressured the Russian space program to add one more. This left no room for spacesuits on board, so this also became the first spaceflight without spacesuits . Two of the crewmembers, an engineer and a doctor, became the first civilians to go to space. On Oct. 12, 1964, the Soviet Union launched the first multiperson mission, Voskhod 1, which launched three Russian cosmonauts into space.

articles.body: Fire erupted in the morning skies over Siberia on June 30, 1908, as an atmospheric explosion occurred that remains unmatched by any similar event in modern history. That day, at approximately 7:15 a.m. local time, observers in Siberia's remote Tunguska region became witnesses to the entry of a brilliant fireball into Earth's atmosphere , trailing smoke across the dawn sky and culminating in a flash brighter than the sun itself. Within seconds, the explosion and resulting shock waves that followed reportedly knocked some members of the nearby Indigenous Evenki population off their feet, and caused damage to dwellings and livestock, while seismic instruments hundreds of miles away logged tremors caused by the blast.
